opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the Rosetta Stone approach is genuinely useful for what it's designed to do. If you want to stitch together lots of benchmarks that were each run on different subsets of models and get a single scale so you can see the overall trend in AI progress over time, a latent "general capabilities" score is a really nice tool. But I'd be a lot more cautious about using it to make fine-grained comparisons between individual models, for a few reasons.

The first is that it compresses everything into one dimension. Any single-number summary assumes that capabilities mostly move together, and at the level of the whole field over several years that's roughly true. But at the level of two specific models released a few months apart, the interesting differences are often precisely the ones a single axis throws away. One model might be much better at agentic coding and long-horizon tasks while another is better at math or knowledge recall. Those can wash out to similar scores while being very different models in practice, and which one is "more capable" depends on what you care about.

Second, the score is only as good as the benchmarks feeding into it, and which benchmarks a given model was evaluated on varies a lot. If one model happens to have been run mostly on older, saturated benchmarks and another on newer, harder ones, the fitted score for each is leaning on quite different evidence. The model is doing its best to put them on a common scale, but the uncertainty for any individual model can be large, and that's easy to lose sight of when you just see a point estimate in a ranking.

Third, there are all the usual benchmark issues that become more acute at the individual-model level: contamination, labs optimizing for particular well-known benchmarks, differences in elicitation, like prompting, scaffolding, how much inference-time compute you allow, and so on. Averaged over many models these effects partially cancel out and you still see the trend. For a single model, one lab's choice to tune hard against a popular benchmark can shift its position noticeably without that reflecting a real underlying difference.

And then finally, there's a gap between benchmark performance and what people actually care about, things like real-world usefulness or, from my perspective, the capabilities relevant to risk: autonomy, ability to do AI R&D, deception-relevant capabilities. A general capabilities score is a reasonable proxy for those in aggregate, but I wouldn't want anyone to say "Model A scores slightly higher than Model B, therefore it's more dangerous" or "more useful." For that kind of question you really want targeted evaluations.

So my overall take is: great for trends and the big picture, and I'm glad people are building these unified scales, but for comparing two particular models, treat it as a rough first pass with fairly wide error bars rather than a definitive ranking.

r001.rationale: The response says it would be cautious about fine-grained comparisons between individual models and treats the score as a rough first pass rather than a definitive ranking.

r002.rationale: The response discusses benchmark optimization generally but does not compare open-source and closed-source models or suggest that open-source models are more overfit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being clear about what that score is actually doing before we talk about what it can't do. The idea in the Rosetta Stone paper is that you take a huge pile of benchmark results across many models, and you fit something like an item response theory model, where each model gets a single latent "ability" number and each benchmark gets parameters for how hard it is and how sharply it discriminates. The nice thing is that it puts benchmarks on a common scale, so you can say something like "MMLU and GPQA are measuring roughly the same underlying thing, just at different difficulty levels." That's genuinely useful for understanding the benchmark landscape.

But I'd be pretty cautious about then turning around and using that single number to rank individual models against each other, for a few reasons.

The first is just that it's a one-dimensional summary. The whole premise is that there's one general factor driving performance, and that works surprisingly well on average across lots of models, but any particular model can deviate from that. A model that's been heavily trained on math and code might be far above its "general" score on those tasks and below on, say, long-context reading or multilingual stuff. The score will tell you the average, and the average can actively mislead you about the specific capability you care about. If you're trying to assess, say, cyber risk or biorisk, the general factor is not the thing you want.

Second, the fit is only as good as the data going in, and the data is a mess. Benchmark results are reported by different labs, with different prompting setups, different numbers of few-shot examples, sometimes with and without tools or chain of thought, sometimes with contamination of the test set in training. Two models can have quite different scores just because one was evaluated more generously. When you aggregate across many benchmarks some of that washes out, but for a single model with a handful of reported numbers, the noise can be large relative to the gap you're trying to resolve between two frontier models.

Third, there's a coverage issue. The models that have been evaluated on the most benchmarks tend to be older or open models. A brand-new frontier model might have results on five or six benchmarks, several of which are saturated, so you're estimating its ability from a very thin and ceiling-limited slice. The method will still spit out a number with some confidence interval, but the interval should be wide, and people tend to quote the point estimate and drop the interval.

Fourth, and this is the one I think about most, the latent scale isn't anchored to anything in the real world. It's defined relative to the population of models and benchmarks in the dataset. So "model A is 0.3 units above model B" doesn't translate into anything you'd care about operationally. It doesn't tell you whether A can do a particular job, or how much more dangerous A would be in the hands of a bad actor. For those questions you need task-specific, ideally real-world or uplift-style evaluations, not a general factor.

And finally, it's inherently backward-looking. The benchmarks that exist were designed for the models that existed when they were written. As capabilities move, the relevant frontier skills are often things that aren't well captured yet, like long-horizon agentic work, or robustness under adversarial pressure. A general score fitted on existing benchmarks will systematically underweight those.

So my overall take is: it's a good tool for making sense of benchmarks, and for a rough sanity check on where a model sits in the broad landscape. I would not use it as the thing that adjudicates whether one lab's model is better than another's, and I definitely wouldn't use it for safety-relevant decisions. For those you need to go look at the specific capabilities you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly cautions against using the general score to rank individual models and explains that it can mislead fine-grained comparisons.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible benchmark contamination and that older or open models have more evaluation results, but does not suggest that open-source models are more overfit to benchmarks than closed-source models.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about treating it as a sufficient summary of an individual model. You’re taking performance across a bunch of benchmarks and compressing it into one number. That can capture a real pattern—models that do well on one benchmark tend to do well on others—without capturing every difference that matters.

Two models could have the same general capabilities score but quite different strengths and weaknesses. If you care about coding, or scientific reasoning, or some particular capability relevant to risk, those differences might be more important than the overall score.

There’s also a question of how well the relationship generalises. If you train a model specifically to be good at one kind of task, you shouldn’t necessarily expect its other capabilities to improve in the way the score would predict. So I’d use it as a useful broad summary, but for a comparison that matters, I’d want to look at the particular capabilities we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that the score is only a broad summary and can hide capability differences between individual models, making it inadequate for fine-grained comparisons.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare open-source and closed-source models or suggest that open-source models are more benchmark-overfit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful as a rough summary, but I’d be pretty cautious about using it to compare two particular models. You’re compressing a whole profile of strengths and weaknesses into one number. Two models can get the same score while being good at quite different things, and those differences might be exactly what you care about.

There’s also a distinction between explaining the variation in the models you studied and having a measure that will generalise to new models. If most of your models improve together on lots of benchmarks, you can capture a lot of that variation with one factor. But that doesn’t establish that every future model will follow the same pattern. A model trained specifically for coding or reasoning could look quite different.

So I’d use the score to get a broad sense of where a model sits, then look at the individual evaluations relevant to the question I’m actually asking. I wouldn’t treat a small difference in that score as establishing that one model is unambiguously more capable than another.

r001.rationale: It advises caution when comparing particular models with one score, noting that the score compresses differing strengths and weaknesses and that small differences do not establish which model is more capable.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about open-source models being more overfit to benchmarks than closed-source models.
